item.title: 358,236 Markets, One Verdict: The Price Is Usually Right
item.description:
358,236 Markets, One Verdict: The Price Is Usually Right

Prediction markets finally have a report card big enough to trust. PredictDesks graded 358,236 resolved markets, 333,464 on Polymarket and 24,772 on Kalshi, against what actually happened. A day before resolution, the favourite won 76.9% of the time, and in standard markets the average gap between price and reality was just 0.9 points on Polymarket and 1.7 on Kalshi.

Strip out the easy questions and the picture sharpens. Two-thirds of Polymarket's sampled markets resolved No, most of them long shots parked at a cent or two. Limit the test to markets priced between 10% and 90% a day out, the genuinely uncertain ones, and the favourite's win rate falls to 65.9%. The headline accuracy is real, but it is flattered by questions nobody was ever unsure about.

What is being forecast matters more than where. Tech and science markets scored a Brier 0.040 a day out on Polymarket; sports, the biggest category on both platforms, scored 0.196, the hardest call on the board. Weighted to the same mix of topics, the two exchanges finished in a dead heat: 0.150 for Polymarket, 0.147 for Kalshi. Across 24 Federal Reserve meetings priced on both, their odds differed by just 0.8 points a day before the decision.

The warning is aimed at the industry's fastest-growing product: templated ladder markets, temperature brackets, spreads, totals and exact scores, now 38% of the sample and 47% of Polymarket's 2026 markets. There, outcomes priced under 10 cents won 1.6 times as often as their prices implied, and favourites priced at 80 to 90 cents won only 76% of the time. In standard markets, long shots were the leak: every $100 spent on contracts below 5 cents returned about $81, before fees.

The rarest line in the data may be the most honest: in just 1.1% of markets, the winner had been priced at 10% or less a day earlier, a list that includes the election of Pope Leo XIV. The crowd is usually right. The study's gift is showing exactly where it is not.

item.title: 70 Percent, a Record: Two Days Out, the Market Prices a Sweep
item.description:
70 Percent, a Record: Two Days Out, the Market Prices a Sweep

Kalshi's balance-of-power contract put the chance of Democrats winning both the House and the Senate at 70 percent on Sunday, an all-time high and up more than nine points in a month. Polymarket priced the same sweep at 72 percent. In early September the Kalshi contract sat below 50 percent.

The alternatives are fading. A split Congress, with Democrats taking the House and Republicans retaining the Senate, priced at 27 percent on Kalshi and 23 percent on Polymarket. A Republican sweep priced at 6 percent on Kalshi and 5 percent on Polymarket.

The chamber math explains the gap. Kalshi put Democratic control of the House at 93.2 percent and the Senate at 71 percent, with Polymarket at 72 percent on the Senate. DeFi Rate put the combined Senate price up six points this week. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and the 51st seat runs through Maine, where Troy Jackson priced at 69 percent, up eight points in seven days.

The money and the ballots are moving together. Traders put $17 million into election markets in the past 24 hours, according to DeFi Rate. Of 53.9 million early ballots cast, 46 percent came from Democrats and 35 percent from Republicans. Nate Silver's generic ballot showed Democrats ahead by 9.1 points, 52.4 percent to 43.3 percent.

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3. Two days out, the market is not pricing a close finish for control of Congress. It is pricing a sweep, at a record price, and leaving the split outcome as the only real alternative.

Sources: Kalshi News, DeFi Rate, Seeking Alpha

item.title: Maryland Said No. Traders Traded Its Elections Anyway
item.description:
Maryland Said No. Traders Traded Its Elections Anyway

Maryland law is not ambiguous. Election Law Section 16-902 says a person may not bet on the outcome of an election: a misdemeanor, a fine of $50 to $500, and the stake forfeited to the county. In March the State Board of Elections warned that gambling on elections is illegal in Maryland.

The markets traded anyway. As of about 9:15 AM ET on Sunday, Polymarket's 20 Maryland markets had recorded about $599,500 in volume, covering the governor's race, all eight House districts, turnout, margins and a redistricting measure. The busiest was the 1st District at about $98,800, with Rep. Andy Harris at about 86.5% against about 12% for Dan Schwartz. The governor's market carried about $30,500, with Gov. Wes Moore at about 99%.

Kalshi tells the same story in contracts: about 400,500 traded across 27 Maryland events. The governor market alone traded about 303,000 — about 199,000 on Republican nominee Dan Cox and about 104,000 on Moore, Cox last at 1 cent and Moore at 99 cents, with about 70,900 Cox contracts changing hands in the prior 24 hours. A one-cent longshot piles up contracts without piling up cash.

The state is escalating. Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis asked the state prosecutor in July to investigate whether the contracts violate the ban, and in September the board barred election officials, judges and contractors from holding them. Kalshi disputes that state law applies, saying a regulator and a Washington court have determined these markets are legal under the federal system.

Two days before the vote, Maryland is the national fight in miniature: the state is also litigating Kalshi's sports contracts, while CNN estimates 2026 election trading on Kalshi and Polymarket at more than $750 million. The ban is on the books. So are the prices.

Sources: RG, Capital Gazette, Maryland Matters

The contract measures a touch of the level during the month, not a month-end close above it. (TokenPost)
